newsitem.title: UK: EMRGING MARKET OUTLOOK-Balkan unrest, Brazil vote.
newsitem.headline: EMRGING MARKET OUTLOOK-Balkan unrest, Brazil vote.

text.p: Political unrest in the Balkans, a crucial vote in Brazil's congress, and the impact of Nigeria's long-delayed budget announcement will give focus to emerging debt and equity markets in the week ahead.

But these events will unfurl against a backdrop of uncertainty about U.S. interest rates, again governing investor sentiment across the developing world, as players scrutinise Tuesday's speech by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan for any hint of an imminent rate rise.

"Some think the risk of a rate rise has gone up and there are fewer profit warnings from U.S. companies, which makes us very nervous," said one emerging market equity strategist here. "We continue to watch every number out of the United States."
Stocks in MEXICO, which sends the bulk of its exports to the United States, and ARGENTINA with its currency pegged to the dollar, will be most strongly affected by any rate rise.
Meanwhile more immediate pressures mount in the Balkans, where attempts to reverse BULGARIA's virtual economic collapse remain paralysed by political deadlock.
Petar Stoyanov, sworn in as president on Sunday, used his inaugural speech to back opposition calls for early elections, and London-based investors are anxious to see an end to the uncertainty.

"The question is whether the election will be in June, or October or December," said Parvoleta Shtereva, emerging market analyst at ING Barings. "I don't think that anything beyond June will be a real solution because (the crisis) will just drag on."
But fears Bulgaria may default on the January 28 payment of $135 million in Brady interest dues were receding after Sofia decided to borrow the funds, she said.
"There is almost no doubt they will pay the January coupon -- they have the money, they have the willingness to pay," she said. "Now eveyone is now looking to (the next coupon in) July."
While the borrowed funds have to be returned by year-end, investors are hoping the country will have made progress by then on selling-off state-owned firms, one condition for IMF help.
"We haven't heard much about their fire sale," Shtereva said.

Debt market players will also be monitoring political unrest in SERBIA as nine weeks of demonstrations show no sign of abating. Protesters are pressing President Slobodan Milosevic to reverse the cancellation of local election results.
But analysts see little impact on Serbia's outstanding debt, with no movement on restructuring likely until well into 1997.
However the award of foreign currency debt ratings to CROATIA last week will promote further demand for its paper.
That will be boosted by roadshows this week for its debut Eurobond -- a $250 million five-year issue expected to be launched on February 6.
The international debt market is also gearing up for a $2 billion dual-tranche global bond for ARGENTINA. Trading in its other debt instruments was quashed in anticipation last week.

Meanwhile BRAZIL heads into a crucial week with the lower house of Congress set to take its first full vote on a key constitutional amendment allowing Fernando Henrique Cardoso to realise his dream of standing for a second term as president.
"Everyone thinks it will be passed but the concern is at what price," said one Latin American equity analyst here, pointing to the political horse-trading preceding the vote.

The Brazilian stock market registered above-average volumes last week on optimism over the amendment, which will give Brazil a chance of implementing long-overdue structural reforms that will benefit its telecom and electricity utilities especially.
Debt market players will also be digesting news from NIGERIA which on Sunday presented its delayed 1997 budget shorn of expected moves towards economic liberalisation.
One analyst described the budget as a "lost opportunity" as it contained no moves to attract foreign investment via privatisation.
"That is Nigeria's only macro-economic statement for the year and people will be disappointed," said one emerging market economist.
Spreads on Nigerian "Par" Brady bonds were unlikely to tighten further since investors would compare them unfavourably with their Argentine counterparts, she added.
"It is a simple choice between Nigeria and Argentina."
After a phenomenal rise of nearly 22 percent last week, COLOMBIA's stock market looks set to power ahead, though some investors are growing restive after totting up good returns.
"We are overweight in our asset allocation, it is a market we like, but now we are looking for weakness," said one Latin American fund manager here.
But after last year's poor performance Colombia was still one of the region's cheapest markets, she added.
Investors are now looking ahead to Washington's March 1 decision on whether to decertify the country again for not participating actively enough in the anti-drug war.
Some say this looks unlikely after a series of measures Bogota has implemented over the past year.

Among Asian markets, KOREAN global depositary receipts have held up well despite the country's industrial unrest, and traders and funds say they are bullish on its financial sector and on some domestic plays.
The IFC emerging market composite investable index, IFC/IPRD, denominated in dollars, was up 2.0 percent week on week at 312.71 points on Monday.
Latin America was up 3.7 percent at 589.11, Asia was up 0.5 percent at 260.68, and Europe, the Middle East and Africa were up 2.5 percent at 143.48.
